title: Detecting Abnormal SharePoint Data Mining by Privileged or Rare Users
shortTitle: Detecting Abnormal SharePoint Data Mining by Privileged o...
summary: This strategy detects abnormal data mining in SharePoint, where a user or service account reads far more documents, sites and lists than its role requires. The signal is volume plus breadth: many downloads and access events across many site collections in a short period, supported by search queries for sensitive terms and by a client address the account has never used. Telemetry comes from cloud file sharing audit records, search query logs, identity sign in records and data loss prevention alerts. It fails in practice because site migrations, legal discovery and records retention jobs produce the same pattern, so the acting account and its business approval must be checked before anyone escalates.

beginner.definition: SharePoint is a place where teams store and share documents online. This detection looks for a user who reads far more of it than usual. It catches bulk downloading, wide site listing and heavy search use. The goal is to spot data collection before the files leave the company.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most company knowledge sits in file sharing platforms such as SharePoint. An attacker with one valid account can copy thousands of files without using any exploit at all. That collection step stays quiet if nobody watches the volume. Early detection gives you time to block the account and reset its credentials.
howItWorks: SharePoint writes an audit record for each file access, download and search query.
The rule counts records for each user over a rolling window, such as one hour.
It compares the count with the normal pattern for that user and that site.
It also counts how many different sites and libraries the user touched.
Sign in records add the client address and the device that was used.
A rare user with high volume and wide breadth raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a public library. Most visitors borrow two or three books and leave within ten minutes. One visitor arrives with a trolley, walks every aisle and fills it in ten minutes flat. He has done nothing illegal, because he holds a valid card. The librarian still remembers him, because the pattern is strange. This detection is the librarian watching the aisles.
takeaways: Volume and breadth together are a stronger signal than either one alone.
Compare each user with their own history, not only with the team average.
Check the client address and the device before you escalate an alert.

objectives: Describe how SharePoint records file access, download and search activity.
Explain why volume plus breadth is a useful scoring method.
Build a per user baseline for document access over thirty days.
Correlate audit records with sign in data for the same account.
Write a pseudo-rule with a threshold and a service account filter.
dataSources: Cloud file sharing audit records for file accessed, file downloaded and file synced operations, with site and library names
Search query audit records with the query text, the result count and the searching account
Identity provider sign in logs with source address, client application and conditional access result
Data loss prevention alerts recording large outbound transfers from cloud storage
Site collection administration audit records for permission changes and permission enumeration
logic: The pattern is a single account reaching a volume and breadth of content that its own history does not explain. Analysts correlate the account identifier and the client address across file access, download, search and sign in records, then compare counts with a per user baseline for the same weekday and hour. Normal power users repeat the same few sites daily, while migration and backup accounts move whole libraries in a steady planned way from a known service address. The malicious or insider case shows a first time client address, a burst of downloads across many sites the account never used, search queries for terms such as payroll or confidential, and no matching business project on record.
pseudoQuery:
# title: SharePoint Bulk Document Access by Rare User Account
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: sharepoint
# detection:
#   selection:
#     Operation:
#       - 'FileDownloaded'
#       - 'FileAccessed'
#   filter_service:
#     UserId|endswith: '-migration'
#   condition: selection and not filter_service
# level: high
falsePositives: Legal discovery project that copies thousands of documents for an ongoing case
Site migration performed by an approved service account outside business hours
A new team member granted access to a large document library and reading it for the first time
Automated records retention tool that enumerates and copies site content on a nightly schedule
tuningNotes: Set the threshold from a per user baseline of at least thirty days, and express it as a multiple of the user's own daily downloads rather than a fixed count. Scope the rule to sites that hold sensitive data, and exclude migration, legal hold and records management accounts by name pattern. Add a filter for users who are new to a site and whose access was approved by a manager. This removes most of the noise, but you lose some coverage of a slow insider who stays just under the threshold by spreading the collection over several weeks.
